en: Sutta Nipāta 4.6 Jarāsutta Brief indeed is this life;
One dies even before a hundred years have passed;
and even if one lives beyond that,
one still dies through old age.
People grieve for what they have claimed as their own,
for possessions are never permanent;
this world is indeed characterized by separation.
Having seen this, one should not dwell in a home.
Even by death is abandoned that which a man thinks, "This is mine."
Having understood this as well, a wise person,
my follower, should not bow down out of attachment,
just like a meeting in a dream.
A man who has awakened does not see [the dream];
even so, one does not see a beloved person who has passed away and died.
Those people, whether seen or heard of,
whose names are here pronounced—
of them only the name shall remain.
For this person who still has something to be told,
those greedy for what they claim as "mine" do not abandon sorrow, lamentation, and stinginess.
Therefore, the sages, seeing safety,
went forth having abandoned possessions.
For the bhikkhu who lives in seclusion,
For one who frequents a secluded seat, it is said that this is their harmony:
he who does not display himself for the sake of existence.
In all things the sage is independent;
he does nothing that is pleasing, nor anything that is displeasing;
in him there is neither lamentation nor stinginess.
Just as water does not cling to a leaf,
just as a drop of water on a lotus leaf,
or just as water does not cling to a lotus flower;
Thus the sage is not defiled by what is seen,
heard, or thought; for the one who is free from worldly attachments does not conceive pride because of them.
Namely, regarding what is seen, heard, or thought:
one does not seek purity through anything else,
for such a person neither becomes attached nor becomes dispassionate.
The Jarā Sutta is the sixth.
